Both Lacan and Agamben are interested in the thought of an absolute alterity beyond the categories of ‘us and them’ - an otherness that may prevail beyond the law and language, the law as language. She is the author of The Reproduction of Evil: A Clinical and Cultural Perspective.

Frankfurter's book, Evil Incarnate, is a scholarly, interdisciplinary work grounded in meticulous research. Moving through history and across cultures, the author meditates on mankind's darkest imaginings about the nature of Otherness. Entwining religious studies, cultural studies and psychoanalysis, Frankfurter articulates the recurrent myth of ‘evil incarnate’. This is a fictive theatre of demonic practices, through which the Other infiltrates our goodness. The author suggests that, in moments of social crisis, collective vision tends to conjure the Other's religious practices as a series of ritual inversions, perversions and monstrosities. This is a projective percept, in which the violation of our taboos is attributed to the Other.

This phenomenon changes throughout history, and, yet, it retains certain motifs. It imagines the Other as formalizing malignant spiritual rituals: orgies, incest, bloodletting and cannibalism; the sacrifice of our children on the altar of Satan. In the myth of ‘evil incarnate’, such practices refuse to stay at the margins. They insinuate themselves into ‘us’ through invisible, and unholy predations. Once a culture is convinced that there is a demonic presence, mass panics and persecutions ensue. In the process, ‘evidence’ is produced by performative role taking. ‘Evidence’ is ‘found’ by self-anointed exorcist-priests, who gain power and social stature through their unique capacity to detect unseen ‘evil’. ‘Evidence’ is confessed under torture; it is proffered by ‘victims’ in the sway of mass hysteria. It is entered as fact into histories, ethnographies and religious texts. Then these texts legitimize the next ‘discovery’ of demonic presence.

Frankfurter's thesis is sustained by exhaustive references to the medieval witch hunts and the Jewish blood libel. But his particular focus is the satanic ritual abuse (SRA) panic that occurred in the United States in the 1990s. His persuasive argument is that SRA accusations were only the most recent form of this recurrent trope. Extensive investigation by law enforcement never produced any evidence for such a cult. In Frankfurter's view, the SRA epidemic was multiply determined. It was, in part, a deflection from familial sexual abuse. It is his contention that there has never been any evidence of a religious group (or cult) that actually formalizes the ritual practices attributed to ‘evil incarnate’. Instead, he suggests that demonization, persecution and purification focus psychosocial anxieties, and offer them some type of resolution. This view is articulated with reference to Kleinian psychoanalytic formulations. It has a natural resonance with the cultural vision offered to us by theorists and psychoanalysts who have studied destructiveness, such as Alford (1989), Grand (2000), Altman (2005), and Peltz (2005).

Romanticism anticipates Freud in its advocacy of something like a talking cure. William Wordsworth, for example, in discussing his long autobiographical Prelude, acknowledges that it is ‘a thing unprecedented in Literary history that a man should talk so much about himself’ (1967, p. 586). Elsewhere Wordsworth names as a ‘reasonable’ prerequisite for his poetic production the ‘review of his own Mind’ (2007, p. 38). In Romantic Psychoanalysis: The Burden of the Mystery, Joel Faflak considers the degree to which Romanticism's anticipation of the psychoanalytic project produces a kind of primal scene for psychoanalysis.

Popular film is an important and effective ideological apparatus and has the potential not only to reinforce subjectivity but also to expose the workings of ideology. Within a psychoanalytic framework, this paper examines the recent historical/fantasy film 300 to assess the demands of ideology on the subject, the political consequences of the form of subjectivity that is affirmed, and the potential of this film to rationalize attitudes that provide justification for present conflict such as the War on Terror. Through this analysis, the article explores the reproduction of subjectivity and, significantly, how it can be challenged.

Murray Schwartz

Murray Schwartz  

Robert Samuels, a lecturer in the UCLA Writing Programs, is concerned that anti-Semitism, the Holocaust and other genocidal traumas are being trivialized and misrepresented in contemporary American culture. His book takes aim at the various ways Samuels thinks popular culture aids and abets this trivialization, and seeks to correct his students' unconscious participation in the erasure of meaning he purports to have found. Using psychoanalytic terminology and concepts of his own invention, he proposes nothing less than ‘a new model of education’ (p. 5) intended to overcome student resistances to learning. Samuels believes ‘that most of our colleges and universities feed the rhetorical defense mechanisms that our students have learned from popular culture, and these defensive structures call for universalized indifference, personal passivity, idealized authority, and assimilated prejudices and stereotypes’ (p. 7). ‘The main thesis of this work,’ he writes, ‘is that an effective way to teach the ethical lessons of the Holocaust in contemporary classrooms is to articulate and overcome the central defense mechanisms shaping students’ resistances to critical thinking and positive social change' (p. 3). This ambitious project, part of a series of publications called ‘Education, Psychoanalysis and Social Transformation,’ comes with high praise in jacket blurbs from reputable faculty in literature and applied psychoanalysis.

Unfortunately, Samuels' performance does not live up to its billing. Despite his admirable commitment to progressive education, throughout this short but repetitive book Samuels' insights into the misrepresentations of the Holocaust compete with terminological confusion, distorted and tendentious arguments, unsupported assertions and a myopic view of Holocaust education in America. To illustrate the nature and extent of the book's limitations, let me give some examples.

Samuels claims that four defense mechanisms account for resistance to a proper understanding of the Holocaust. Although he recognizes that defenses are essential to personal development and cultural life, his focus is on the ways they prevent the truth of the trauma from emerging. He calls these mechanisms ‘empathic identification,’ ‘idealization,’ ‘universalization’ and ‘assimilation.’ Following Aristotle, he further claims that these defenses operate at the social level as ‘rhetorical’ tropes. The trick is to avoid confronting his students' defenses directly by using these terms ‘as rhetorical figures and not as psychological or political processes’ (p. xi). If not psychological or political processes, what are they? In fact, Samuels does use his terms to name individual and collective psychological defenses throughout his text, simply attaching the word ‘rhetorical’ to the idea of defense, which he gets from the ego-psychological dimension of Freud's writings.

asylum-migration nexus; ethno-mimesis; recognition; praxis

This paper presents a 10-year trajectory of research in the United Kingdom exploring the asylum-migration nexus and processes of belonging using participatory and arts-based methodologies. The relational dynamics involved in exploring the space between ethnography and arts-based practice (ethno-mimesis) are viewed through the work of critical theorists Theodor Adorno and Walter Benjamin. These psychoanalytic critical theorists provide a framework for thinking through the relationship between art and society, participatory research and the politics of representation.

Steven Groarke  

Presented as a kind of conversation between Leo Bersani and Adam Phillips, Intimacies is a book about couples. Three couples, in particular, animate the conversation: the Socratic couple in the Phaedrus, Freud's analytic couple, and the mother-infant couple. Bersani is particularly interested in the first of these three couples; Phillips introduces mothers and babies into the conversation; and they both share an interest in the analytic couple, albeit for different reasons. The nursing couple may be seen here as a prototype of the talking couples, who, in turn, represent two contrasting paradigms of intimacy. Like most things said in conversation, the book is not well argued; things tend to be left up in the air, and, as Phillips himself says in his opening remarks, the book is ‘neither diligent, thorough, researched, nor finished’ (p. viii). Readers expecting to find an index, a bibliography, or referenced citations will be frustrated. Moreover, the inevitable gaps and uncertainties are allowed to stand as the conversation unfolds, making no sacrifice à la Freud (1933) ‘to an appearance of being simple, complete or rounded-off’ (p. 6).

That the authors each focus only on what interests them consolidates Intimacies' rough-and-ready, freewheeling quality; it is also the reason why I think the book is worth reading. There is a spontaneous feel throughout that extends from the conversational style to the main themes of the book. Bersani and Phillips are trying to feel their way toward what I would call an improvised sense of intimacy. In a characteristically pointed phrase, Phillips defines psychoanalysis as talk without sex. Bersani begins by elaborating on this idea from a different angle, approaching the analytic dialogue as more than simply a non-sex contract. Essentially, Bersani treats psychoanalysis as as a problem of knowledge. And he is indebted here to Foucault's (1971) critique of ‘knowledge’ (connaissance) in terms of ‘the will to knowledge’ (la volonté de savoir). Like Foucault, Bersani seems to be grappling throughout with ‘new relational modes’, or new ways of being together with one another, as historical modalities of reason as well as relations of power.

In his most recent book, Calvin Thomas examines the relationship between abjection and masculinity first explored in his 1996 book, Male Matters: Masculinity, Anxiety, and the Male Body on the Line. Whereas that book devoted a considerable degree of attention to fluidic abjection (piss and Hegel, semen and the pornographic money-shot), this book maintains a “tighter focus” on the anus and “whatever figuratively falls in and out of it” (p. xiv). Similarly, while Male Matters investigated a variety of “theorists of difference,” here the author concentrates primarily on developing lively dialogues with the psychoanalytic thinking of Jacques Lacan and “the thoughts on abjection that fall in and out of his writing” (p. xv).

The book contains six main essays, along with an introduction and a substantial section of notes that is worthy of a close read. As a collection of essays, rather than a work of developmental chapters, the pieces do not build toward proving a temporally situated cultural argument as such. Rather, as Thomas indicates in the opening pages, the essays are, foremost, discrete “adventures in abjection” (p. xi). True to this spirit, while all the entries share a concern for abjection in theory and representational practice, they shamelessly flit across theoretical and disciplinary boundaries, beginning with a review of the author's prior research and appropriately skidding to a halt with an interpretation of the death drive.

In the introduction, Thomas outlines his working definition of abjection as “a problem of writing, as a disturbance in the relation between identity and its representation” (p. xvi). The tensions implied by this understanding are subjected to scrutiny in the six chapters that follow. In “Beginning with a Bit of (Be)Hindsight…” Thomas looks back to his earlier work, while rehearsing the recent contributions of Judith Butler, Lee Edelman, and Slavoj Žižek (among others) to the overlapping discourses of psychoanalysis and sexuality. He does so to lay a foundation for thinking about the production of men's bodies as “the manner in which men's bodies are produced and the matters that men's bodies do produce” (p. 2). Thomas deftly moves from complex critical theory to pop culture to reveal the neutralization of black masculinity next to white masculinity in Janet Jackson's music video Love Will Never Do (For You) and Oliver Stone's Any Given Sunday, and to stress that no act of representation is extricable from the material, socio-cultural production of men's bodies.

Jeffrey Murer

Jeffrey Murer  

Those who hope to ameliorate situations of collective violence often aim to get the various participants and parties in a conflict to come to see one another as more similar than different. If only Israelis would spend more time with Palestinians, Georgians with Russians, Serbs with Croats and so on, the conflicts would abate because each side would understand more about the other. Adrian Millar's Socio-Ideological Fantasy and the Northern Ireland Conflict questions this assumption of minimizing conflict through encounter by suggesting that the source of the conflict may have far more to do with the ways a given community or collectivity sees itself than it has to do with how it sees the other. Millar offers a new and refreshing take on the Northern Ireland conflict specifically, and collective conflicts more generally, through the application of Lacanian psychodynamic theory.

In contrast to more traditional approaches to conflict resolution, Millar suggests that often ‘… getting the subject to change his/her perception of the other is not the way to succeed’ (p. 32). Rather, he suggests that the subject perceives the other in particular ways as part of a dynamic process of psychological defences, namely, those of projection and splitting, by which a subject responds to a sense of vulnerability, or threat, or (in Lacanian terms) lack by constructing a mirroring other. It is into this mirroring other that the self projects unwanted traits, thereby creating a new, unified subjectivity. The new self is most fully realized in the ‘not self’; the I is best understood in the terms of ‘not-I’. However, the recognition of the distinction between self and other is also the basis of an imaginary relationship within the subject. Millar suggests that this imaginary relationship always involves violence as the conflicted, complicated, insecure self fantasises that the other he encounters is whole, complete and secure. Millar asserts that, for Lacan, conflict is never about competition or disagreement, but rather is a matter of domination and oppression (p. 16). The relationship then becomes based on ‘intimidation, aggression, aggressive competitiveness, superiority, jealousy, and resentment’ that the self feels toward the other (p. 15). ‘Conflict management therefore needs to talk about aggression’ (p. 31).

The Medicalization of Society, The Loss of Sadness, and Shyness mark a shift in the way contemporary Western culture determines which human behaviors are considered disorders. With growing concern, the authors trace the way behaviors previously characterized as “normal” (like shyness) are increasingly diagnosed as disorders; and they investigate with equal concern the degree to which medications, including powerful psychotropic drugs, are prescribed to treat these disorders. While definitions of “normal” are dependent on particular historical and cultural contexts, the authors of the titles reviewed here note the disappearance of the idea of “normal” human emotions (like sorrow), behaviors (like shyness), and physical attributes (like baldness or short stature). Collectively, the authors invoke a future in which the range of acceptable human emotions is so narrow that disordered (and therefore medicalized) is the new “normal.” Although the authors are careful to acknowledge that the lives of those suffering from Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), for example, are often improved immeasurably by diagnosis and treatment, the authors also wonder what risks attend the expanding definition of “disordered.” What does the expansion of the label “disordered” tell us about contemporary culture, its defenses, its resistances, and its own disorder(s)?

By Peter Conrad (Harry Coplan Professor of Social Sciences at Brandeis University), The Medicalization of Society has the largest scope of the titles under consideration. Conrad does not limit his focus to the history of a particular disorder but instead addresses four case studies, which, when taken together, mark an expanding use of medicine to treat a variety of human conditions, “problems” that even two decades ago would not have been deemed appropriate for medication.

From the isolation of the hospital bed to the specialization of the mortuary, the experiential dynamics of grief and dying are largely excluded from the American public sphere. And yet death persists and proliferates in the entertainment and news industries in the form of virtual spectacle. Through an examination of the popular television series Six Feet Under, this study explores the place of representation in inciting, challenging and sustaining expressions of anxiety and social repression surrounding the experience of death and grief in contemporary life. For some time now, the study of Victorian literature in the United States has been dominated by various strains of historicist scholarship. In few fields has Frederic Jameson's famous injunction to ‘always historicize’ (Jameson, 1981, p. 9) been taken up with such seriousness as it has in Victorian studies. Yet while many of the most brilliant and startling analyses of nineteenth-century culture have come out of Marxist-materialist and new historicist traditions over the past quarter of a century or so, the notion of ‘history’ that typically informs recent scholarship is surprisingly limited - and limiting. Even though new historicist work claims to recognize the problematic nature of the relationship between narrative and ‘reality,’ it is frequently beset by a literal-mindedness that seeks to authenticate texts by retrieving their referents in nonliterary, and hence ‘realer,’ contexts. Thus conceived (and in spite of the precautions taken by such precursors to the new historicism as Michel Foucault), ‘history’ tends to authorize new and rigid narratives of truth and causality. Not surprisingly, typically excluded in Victorian studies are views of history that emphasize ambivalence, irrationality and the impossibility of getting an ultimate handle on the real.

In his bold and original study, Jason B. Jones argues that Victorian writers had, ironically, a much more nuanced conception of history than historicist scholars today appreciate or have access to themselves. The texts he reads - principally, Thomas Carlyle's The French Revolution, Dickens's Barnaby Rudge and A Tale of Two Cities, Charlotte Brontë's Shirley and George Eliot's Felix Holt, the Radical and Middlemarch - understand historical causes as ultimately unknowable (or ‘lost’) and resistant to single meanings. Not content to choose between the fantasy that humans author their own identities and the fantasy that they are authored by forces beyond their control, the nineteenth-century writers Jones studies illuminate the need to pursue historical explanations even as they take history itself to be a constantly receding cause. Instead of eluding the demands of historical realism, as they are often taken to task for doing, the authors of these texts elude, in Jones's view, the demands of a solipsistic and impoverished theoretical perspective.

Gal Gerson   Associate Professor at the School of Political Science - Department of Government and Political Theory, the University of Haifa. He is the author of books on liberal theory and the history of liberalism, and articles on liberalism, feminism, and psychoanalysis.
feminism; motherhood; object relations; I.D. Suttie

Widely acknowledged as an inspiration and early model for the British object relations school, Ian Suttie's work illustrates both the school's advantages and its pitfalls. Suttie's work includes a core concept of matriarchy as the social order best suited for healthy upbringing. As object relations theory has attracted both praise and criticism from feminists for its perceptions of gender and the family, examining Suttie's notion of matriarchy may serve as a test case for the relationist approach to gender and its links to wider political questions. I argue that Suttie provides some insights that will later be appropriated and further developed by key feminist thinkers. His position, however, implies an essentialist foundation that makes family relations hierarchic and non-negotiable. The structured household and its gendered division of labor is the cornerstone of Suttie's utopia.

The primary task of an ideology, Hinshelwood says, is to promote ‘devotion to, and survival of, ideas held by the group’. How does it happen, then, that an idea can become such a powerful dimension of the psyche that people are willing to kill and die for it? In this paper I examine how people attach to ‘sacred objects’ that are conceived as more significant than the self. Collective forms of violence are generated on the basis of a perception of ‘enemies’ that are imagined to be acting to destroy a sacred object that constitutes the foundation for one's society. Enemies represent that which is separate from the self - and they challenge the group's fantasy of omnipotence. People kill and die in the name of defending their fantasy of omnipotence. We become capable of doing so at the moment we begin to abandon our own identification with ideologies conceived as omnipotent.

Psychoanalytic social theorists who work in the relational tradition have analyzed the psychodynamics of enemy systems and identified persistent themes in the operation of these systems. Although enemy systems often involve enmity between ethnic, national or cultural groups, the psychodynamic symptoms of such systems are observable when social groups cast familiar outgroups as enemies. This paper examines the process by which enemies are created in the midst of conflict. Rather than accepting the premise that the parties to a conflict exist a priori and are set against one another once the ‘proper’ conditions exist, the paper argues that group-selves and enemy-others are created in the wake of a collective identity crisis. Under conditions of threat, collectivities may engage in a process best described by Julia Kristeva as abjection, whereby a group will cast off a familiar yet foreign part of the self and project into this severed part those unwanted or undesirable traits associated with vulnerability. This process of splitting is both trauma and response to trauma; as such the process is impossible to describe as it occurs. A proxy narrative, created to make sense of the process to the anxious and threatened group-self, presents a narrative of the conflict between the group-self and the enemy-other that does not acknowledge the previous relationship between the two. It is only through processes similar to adaptive mourning that a collectivity can come to question the content of a proxy narrative and re-evaluate the relationship with the abject-other. Through mourning, a new relationship can be forged and a new narrative of that relationship and its evolution through conflict can be created. Through mourning new futures become available, just as the past is re-evaluated and likewise created anew.

In the mid-1920s, Ernst Simmel created the Schloss Tegel Sanatorium, just outside Berlin, as a place for indigent people with severe psychiatric disorders to be treated psychoanalytically. Simmel's thesis, that impinging social and economic forces are as great a challenge to patients' recovery as are their internal disorders, was well received by like-minded colleagues, including Freud. At Schloss Tegel, a unified clinical and political discourse allowed the psychoanalysts to establish a new praxis based not on the strictures of establishment psychiatry but on an ideology of dialectical materialism. In the end the sanatorium was defeated by chronic underfinancing and ultimately the violent Nazi takeover. What remains, however, is Simmel's rich legacy of psychoanalytic experimentation that confronted the twin predicaments of mental illness and structural oppression.

Caroline Rupprecht has done a remarkable job researching the work of three modernist women writers - Henriette Hardenburg, Djuna Barnes and Unica Zürn - and drawing on the psychoanalytic theory of Freud, Lacan, Klein and others, in order to generate a gender politics that purports to break, if one is to believe the reviewer on the back of the book, ‘preconceived notions of identity and subjectivity through [the] reading of the ‘transgressive potential’ of narcissism.’ Indeed, Rupprecht meticulously reassembles discourses of various kinds - psychoanalysis, literary studies, historical documents and so on - and produces a kaleidoscopic picture of these writers, all of whom, at one point, engaged with and related to identity politics either as a thematic or biographical focus. Rupprecht has produced a veritable ‘Fleissarbeit’ (hard work), divided into two main sections: ‘Paradigms of Narcissism’ and ‘Avant-Garde Women.’

In the first part, Rupprecht outlines with extraordinary sagacity the psychoanalytic theory that has influenced Freud's paper ‘On Narcissism,’ and introduces theorists who, in one way or another, have contributed to the concept of narcissism. In providing a theoretical framework within and against which the author attempts to place the work of the above writers, Rupprecht implicitly underscores the importance of narcissism in the development of psychoanalysis. She ends her introduction by surveying object relations theory and Lacanian psychoanalysis, although, at various moments in her work (for instance, on p. 27), she fails to do justice to the complexity of these theories. Given the scope and range of this ‘Fleissarbeit’ - in fact, nothing seems to escape Rupprecht's critical eye - it is striking that she does not revisit Torok and Abraham's concept of narcissism. To achieve something new, and to provide a comprehensive study of narcissism as a richly layered psychoanalytic and cultural phenomenon - without risking the pitfalls of oversimplification of gender and identity politics - it would have been appropriate to appeal to Torok and Abraham's theory of cryptonymy and anasemia (The Shell and the Kernel, 1994), among others.

This article explores the ways in which class position forms part of immigrants' social imaginary and shapes important aspects of their engagement with the sociocultural landscape to which they have come. It is argued that sociocultural experience is the scaffolding for self-representation across development and thus plays a key role in our conscious and unconscious, in what we do and how we understand it. The story of the South Asian deity Ganesha makes an especially provocative contribution to our insights into the dynamics of subjectivity in general and of masculinity in particular. In combination with clinical psychoanalytic experience, this myth is used to explore and illustrate the following arguments: (1) Our literature too often overlooks the significance of paternal ambivalence toward sons in the dynamics by which male subjectivity develops. (2) Our literature tends to present the root fears that structure human consciousness as either death or castration, which misunderstands the dynamics of ‘deathfulness’ and of ‘castratedness.’ (3) The transgenerational dynamics by which the repressed unconscious is structured deserve more attention than they are usually given. (4) The condition of human subjectivity as castratedness can be usefully comprehended in terms of this subjectivity or consciousness operating as a ‘phallus-that-isn't.’ (5) The attainment of orgasmic genitality depends on the individual's working-through these dynamics. The implications of these insights for any agenda of sociocultural transformation are briefly indicated.

R. Hinshelwood   Member of the British Psychoanalytic Society, a Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists and currently Professor in the Centre for Psychoanalytic Studies, University of Essex, UK. Previously, he was Clinical Director of the Cassel Hospital. He has written extensively on the work of Melanie Klein - Dictionary of Kleinian Thought (1989) and Clinical Klein (1993). He has been interested in the application of psychoanalysis to social science, producing a number of publications including What Happens in Groups (1987), and on therapeutic communities, and more recently Observing Organisations (2000), and a book on psychosis and the dynamics of the psychiatric institution - Suffering Insanity (2004).
ideology; group ideal; personal identity; false consciousness; overvalued idea; selected fact

This paper uses psychoanalytic thinking to understand the way individuals come to be in a social group that develops an ideology. LeBon was one of the earliest to consider destructive groups and the distortion of individuality within crowds and mobs, and his work formed the basis of Freud's thinking. Destructive groups are contrasted with constructive ones that can achieve creative and work-oriented functioning. Destructive groups have various characteristics, one of which is the place that ideas have in the group and in the minds of the members. When ideas become overvalued and thus an ideology, the relation between the individual and the ideas changes. On one hand, in ordinary constructive work and groups, the idea is an abstract notion useable in aspirations and achievements; and on the other hand, in ideological and destructive groups, the individual is equated with the idea, which becomes an end in itself. This movement involves the pressure of social forces upon forms of individual distress that affects their sense of themselves. Following Freud's views on the group ideal, it is possible to understand the excitement in primitive destructive groups, their unreality and the erosion of individuality as coming from the equation of self with the ideal.

Pratyusha Tummala-Narra   Assistant Professor in the Department of Counseling, Developmental, and Educational Psychology at Boston College. She was the founding director of the Asian Mental Health Clinic at Cambridge Health Alliance/Harvard Medical School. She has been a faculty member at Georgetown University School of Medicine and at the Michigan School of Professional Psychology.
immigration; mourning; fantasy; identity; transitional space

Immigrants negotiate the concept of home in multiple ways, including actual visits to the country of origin and recreating in the adoptive land aspects of the country of origin. Fantasies of home as constructed in interpersonal and relational contexts lie at the heart of these visits home. This paper explores the role of fantasy and actual visits home and their relevance to therapeutic process. Case examples illustrate the ways in which real and imagined returns home influence mourning and identity transformation.

Thinking through Others: Cultural Psychology and the Psychoanalytic Treatment of Immigrants

Andrew Harlem PHD

Andrew Harlem

San Francisco, CA, 94103, USA

Andrew Harlem   Associate Professor and Director of Clinical Training in the Doctoral Psychology Program at the California Institute of Integral Studies in San Francisco. Dr. Harlem is President-Elect of the Northern California Society for Psychoanalytic Psychology. He is in private practice in Oakland, CA.
cultural psychology; immigration; culture; psychoanalysis; pluralism

Today's immigrants often have the twenty-first-century desire to maintain the cultural ideals and practices that their predecessors were eager to shed. This paper is concerned with psychoanalytic receptivity to these ideals and practices and, more abstractly, with the conception of cultural difference that informs psychoanalytic theory and practice. The author introduces a conceptual framework from cultural psychology to theorize differences in everyday practice, thought, feeling and relationship patterning across cultures. A case vignette contrasts three potential interpretive responses to a cultural practice that, while common around the world, is relatively unfamiliar to psychoanalysis. It is suggested that a pluralistic conception of difference facilitates modes of listening essential to psychoanalytic work across cultures. In addition, the author suggests that cultural psychology's pluralistic conception of difference may be useful to the psychoanalytic project of theorizing linkages between individual subjectivity, relational phenomena and culture.

large-group identity; cultural amplifiers; suitable targets of externalization; chosen glories; chosen traumas; peaceful coexistence

This paper focuses on ethnic, national, religious and ideological large groups. Large-group identity refers to persistent sameness of tens, hundreds of thousands or millions of individuals, most of whom will never meet during their lifetimes. Within the interactions of large groups, ‘otherness’ is very powerful and is both desirable and frightening. We can enjoy human diversity when we are not preoccupied with the pressures and anxieties associated with the repair and maintenance of our large-group identity. When certain elements of us and them psychology are combined, derivatives of massive aggression surface. Clinicians willing to take part in interdisciplinary efforts have much to offer for those who wish to resolve us and them conflicts.

Kris Yi  

The Brief and Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao tells of the trials and tribulations of Oscar, a black Dominican nerd from New Jersey, and of his mother and her family, whose lives were brutally affected by the political atrocities in her native country. What makes Diaz's novel such a pleasure to read is the way he captures the feel of the English-Spanish bilingual and bicultural world of a segment of urban population in the United States. He accomplishes this by liberal use of both Spanish and English in his book: reading it seems like peeking into an East Los Angeles or Echo Park neighborhood near where I live in Los Angeles. There the people speak the same way Diaz writes in his novel - moving between English and Spanish seamlessly and having so much fun doing it.

That's not all. By peppering his text with numerous references to sci-fi, comic books and fantasy novels and with crude references to women and black men, Diaz makes the young descendants of Dominican immigrants in the contemporary North American ghetto come vividly alive. He showcases their edgy, angry hip-hop machismo (in the person of Yunior); socially maladjusted, sexually awkward, male geekdom (Oscar); and the punk feminism born of humiliation (Lola).

From a psychological standpoint, the book is about political trauma, its impact on a nation of people and on individual lives across generations. For Oscar and his sister, Lola, it all begins with Trujillo, the ‘dictatingest dictator’ the world has ever seen. Diaz's Dominican Republic under Trujillo is a hell on earth: Trujillo is the ultimate lethal narcissist - prone to deadly rages if faced with real or imagined slights (if you speak even slightly ill of him or his relations, you're dead) and who shows no mercy, and certainly no empathy, for his victims. The horror of his regime has an unhinging effect on its citizens, who function in a collective traumatized state - men are only too happy to do his dirty work; ordinary people routinely spy on each other; and apparently normal families buy and sell children with impunity. This state of affairs becomes personal for the family of Oscar's mother (Beli) when her father is arrested for refusing to allow Trujillo to sleep with his daughter, is tortured and then sent away to die. Beli's mother commits suicide soon after, and her two elder sisters are mysteriously murdered. Beli is sold to a family who tortures her and keeps her in a chicken coop until she is rescued by a relative at age 9.

Analysis of an Undocumented Latina Immigrant

Jennifer McCarroll PHD

Jennifer McCarroll

817 Broadway, 9th Floor, New York, NY 10003, USA

Jennifer McCarroll   Graduate of the William Alanson White Adult Psychoanalytic Program, is a member of the editorial board of Contemporary Psychoanalysis. She is in full-time private practice in New York City and has other published papers touching on the topic of culture and psychoanalysis.
psychoanalysis; psychotherapy; immigration; social class; gender roles

This article presents a detailed description of clinical work with an undocumented Latina immigrant living in New York City and a Caucasian-American female analyst. The article focuses on the patient's experience of being an immigrant as that of being second class or lesser than, and how themes of acceptance and rejection by her father and alcoholism in her mother intensified the patient's insecurities around her immigrant status. Issues of social class, gender roles and sibling relationships are also highlighted, both in general and as they played out in the relationship with the analyst.

Salman Akhtar MD

Salman Akhtar   Jefferson Medical College; and Training and Supervising Analyst, Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia.
immigration, friendship, homoethnic enclaves, friends, heteroethnic friends, ethnic foods

In this article I discuss the characteristics that distinguish immigrants' homoethnic friendships from their heteroethnic friendships. I note how the two patterns of socialization serve different psychological functions, at both conscious and unconscious levels. I address the emotionally supportive role of local homoethnic enclaves and the symbolic significance of ethnic food in the context of immigration. I also note, albeit briefly, the ways in which gender differences affect the postmigration socialization processes. Throughout this discourse my main concern would be on the powerful role friendships play in the immigrant's subjectivity.
